core: Cohen and Felson (1979) and the three converging elements: likely offender, suitable target, absence of a capable guardian
The theory explains crime rates and crime events by opportunity structure, holding offender motivation constant
The 1979 puzzle: rising reported predatory crime in the postwar United States, answered by the dispersion of routine activities away from the household
The problem analysis triangle (crime triangle) and its outer ring of controllers: handler, guardian, place manager
Target suitability: VIVA (value, inertia, visibility, access) and CRAVED (concealable, removable, available, valuable, enjoyable, disposable)
Relationship to the rational choice perspective (Cornish and Clarke) and to situational crime prevention
Concentration of crime at very few places; hot spots policing evidence, including the National Academies' Conclusion 4-1
Displacement (five types) versus diffusion of benefits, and the finding that displacement is rarely total
Required rigor: this is an explanation of opportunity, not of criminality; and the victim-blaming misreading of target suitability
supporting: Routine activities defined as recurrent, prevalent activities meeting basic population and individual needs
Hot spot types: crime generators, crime attractors, crime enablers
The 80-20 concentration principle across offenders, victims, places, products, and facilities
The five families of situational crime prevention techniques as set out in the DOJ crime analysis manual
Why detecting displacement is methodologically hard (Barr and Pease caution, quoted in the COPS review)
outOfScope: Strain theory, social learning/differential association, social disorganization, and labeling theory (parallel topics; named and handed off)
Deterrence and incapacitation evidence (owned by what-causes-crime)
Community policing, problem-oriented policing history, and broken windows (owned by community-policing)
Crime measurement systems, UCR/NIBRS/NCVS (owned by crime-data-and-crime-statistics)
Cyber-routine-activity extensions and CPTED design standards

claims.claim: Lawrence Cohen and Marcus Felson set out the routine activity approach in 'Social Change and Crime Rate Trends: A Routine Activity Approach,' American Sociological Review 44(4):588-608, August 1979.
The approach holds that a direct-contact predatory crime requires the convergence in time and space of a likely (motivated) offender, a suitable target, and the absence of a capable guardian.
The theory takes the existence of a likely offender for granted rather than explaining it, and therefore explains crime rates and crime events rather than criminality.

Cohen and Felson's central hypothesis was that the dispersion of activities away from households and families increases the opportunity for crime and so generates higher crime rates; they supported it with data on variables such as labour force participation and household composition.
The problem analysis triangle adds an outer ring of controllers: a guardian for the target, a handler for the offender, and a manager for the place.
Target suitability in the 1979 formulation rests on four attributes summarised by the acronym VIVA: value, inertia, visibility, and access.

Ronald Clarke's 1999 Home Office report Hot Products (Police Research Series, Paper 112) summarises the attributes of frequently stolen goods with the acronym CRAVED - concealable, removable, available, valuable, enjoyable, disposable - and argues that how much a product is stolen may depend critically on ease of disposal.

Situational crime prevention, which grows out of routine activity and rational choice thinking, works on the immediate setting; the DOJ crime analysis manual organises its techniques into increasing the effort, increasing the risks, reducing the rewards, reducing provocations, and removing excuses, and it deliberately targets the perceived risk of capture rather than the severity of punishment.

Crime is highly concentrated at a small number of micro-places: Sherman, Gartin and Buerger reported that 50.4 percent of calls for police service in Minneapolis came from 3.3 percent of addresses in a single year, and Weisburd's 2015 'law of crime concentration' puts the bandwidth at roughly 4 percent of micro-places for 50 percent of crime.

The National Academies' 2018 proactive policing report concludes (Conclusion 4-1) that hot spots policing strategies generate statistically significant crime reduction effects without simply displacing crime into immediately surrounding areas, and that studies measuring displacement tend instead to find a diffusion of crime control benefits into adjacent areas; the report also notes an absence of evidence on long-term and jurisdiction-wide effects.

In the COPS Office systematic review of hot spots policing, 17 of 25 tests examined immediate spatial displacement or diffusion: eight reported significant diffusion of crime control benefits, six reported neither displacement nor diffusion, and only three reported substantial immediate spatial displacement.
Displacement is conventionally divided into five kinds - geographical, temporal, target, tactical, and crime type - and the same categories apply to diffusion of benefits.
Routine activity theory is not a general theory of crime; it focuses on the actions and settings of individuals rather than on neighbourhood characteristics or criminal propensity.

The theory has been criticised in victimology on the ground that it can be read as implying a victim could reduce an offender's motivation by being a less suitable target, and that it assumes an equality of power among victim, offender, and guardian that does not exist.

Hot spot places arise through distinguishable mechanisms - crime generators (large numbers of people drawn for non-criminal reasons), crime attractors (known criminal opportunities), and crime enablers (absent or eroded regulation of behaviour at the place).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Two U.S. Department of Justice publications summarise the same Minneapolis study (Sherman, Gartin and Buerger 1989) with different numbers.
positions: Braga, Papachristos and Hureau (2012, COPS Office) report that 3 percent of Minneapolis addresses accounted for 50 percent of calls for service.
Clarke and Eck's DOJ crime analysis manual reports that 6 percent of Minneapolis addresses accounted for 60 percent of calls for service.
Gill, Wooditch and Weisburd (2017) report the study's figure as 50.4 percent of calls from 3.3 percent of addresses in a particular year.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the most precise figure (50.4 percent of calls from 3.3 percent of addresses), attributes it to the 1989 study as reported by Gill, Wooditch and Weisburd and by the COPS review, and tells students explicitly that summaries of the same study differ - which is itself the point about reading secondary reports of statistics. The full text of the 1989 article could not be retrieved, so it is not registered as a source; the finding is carried by the two sources that report it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How far a change in opportunity displaces rather than prevents crime.
positions: Displacement theory holds that reducing opportunity in one place, time, or target simply moves offending elsewhere.
The empirical reviews find displacement is real but usually partial, and that diffusion of benefits is at least as commonly observed.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states both, gives the COPS review counts, cites the National Academies' Conclusion 4-1, and includes the methodological caution that complete displacement would by construction be hard to detect - so 'rarely total' is a claim about what studies can measure, not a proof that displacement never happens.

positions: Cornish and Clarke's edited volume The Reasoning Criminal: Rational Choice Perspectives on Offending was published in 1986 (Springer-Verlag).
The KPU open textbook dates the perspective to Clarke and Cornish 1987.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the perspective to Cornish and Clarke and dates it to the mid-1980s rather than picking a contested single year.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing substantive about routine activity theory at all: it described the topic as 'a foundational concept in Criminal Justice & Criminology' and offered a toolbox-drawer analogy, a map-legend analogy, and placeholder vocabulary ('context', 'evidence', 'application'). None of it was sourced or specific, and all of it was discarded.
The draft's implied claim that the topic is a definition to be recited and applied to 'a simple scenario' misstates what the theory is for; it is a framework for analysing crime events and rates.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual theory: Cohen and Felson (1979), the three converging elements, and the crime-rate rather than criminality claim.
Added the crime triangle and its outer ring of controllers (handler, guardian, place manager) from the DOJ crime analysis manual and the ASU POP Center.
Added target suitability schemes (VIVA, CRAVED) with their correct originators and dates.
Added the place-based evidence base: crime concentration figures, hot spots policing, National Academies Conclusion 4-1, and the displacement/diffusion counts from the COPS systematic review.
Added the required rigor points as Common Mistakes: that this explains opportunity rather than criminality, and that reading target suitability as victim responsibility is a misuse.
Added the explicit educational-material statement required for this subject and kept the lesson free of any policy position.
rightsIssues: Cohen and Felson (1979) is paywalled. Only bibliographic metadata (Crossref) and the published abstract (ERIC EJ210358) were retrieved; no full text was read and no wording is reproduced.

Clarke's Hot Products (1999) is Crown copyright; the copy read was the PDF hosted by the ASU Center for Problem-Oriented Policing. Treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and only the CRAVED acronym - a term of art - is used, with attribution.

The COPS Office publications were authored under cooperative agreements by non-federal authors, so federal public-domain status is not assumed; both are treated as REFERENCE_ONLY and no wording is reproduced.
The two KPU Introduction to Criminology chapters are CC BY 4.0; they are attributed in the source records, but the lesson prose is original and adapts no sentences.

Gill, Wooditch and Weisburd (2017) is a paywalled Springer article; the author copy hosted by George Mason University's Center for Evidence-Based Crime Policy was read, and the canonical DOI is registered.

sourceRecords.title: Crime Analysis for Problem Solvers in 60 Small Steps
sourceRecords.provider: Ronald V. Clarke and John E. Eck / U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Community Oriented Policing Services
sourceRecords.notes: Full 148-page PDF downloaded from the COPS Office resource centre and read as extracted text on 2026-08-19. Primary source for: routine activity theory as the origin of the problem analysis triangle and its statement that the theory takes the existence of a likely offender for granted; the outer ring of controllers (guardian, handler, manager) with their definitions and examples; the rational choice framing that offenders seek benefit without careful planning; the five types of displacement; diffusion of benefits and its examples; the three mechanisms behind hot spot places (generators, attractors, enablers); the 80-20 concentration principle; and the five families of situational crime prevention techniques (steps 39-43). Also the source for the statement that Cohen and Felson linked rising 1960s-70s residential burglary partly to more women working outside the home. Authored under cooperative agreement 2003-CKWX-048, so federal public-domain status is not assumed; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Testing the 'Law of Crime Concentration at Place' in a Suburban Setting: Implications for Research and Practice, Journal of Quantitative Criminology 33(3):519-545 (September 2017)
sourceRecords.provider: Charlotte Gill, Alese Wooditch, and David Weisburd / Springer
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record verified through the Crossref API (Gill, Wooditch, Weisburd; Journal of Quantitative Criminology 33(3):519-545, September 2017). The author copy hosted by George Mason University's Center for Evidence-Based Crime Policy was downloaded and read as extracted text. Source for the reported figures of the law of crime concentration: Sherman et al. (1989) found 50.4 percent of Minneapolis calls for service came from 3.3 percent of addresses in a particular year; in Seattle 5.1 percent of street segments accounted for 50 percent of crime; Weisburd (2015, his 2014 Sutherland Address) concluded that the bandwidth of concentration is roughly 4 percent of micro-places at 50 percent of crime and under 1.5 percent at 25 percent; and the authors' own finding that 2 percent of street segments in suburban Brooklyn Park, Minnesota produced 50 percent of crime. Also cited here for the statement that high street-by-street variability is one reason focused policing shows little displacement to neighbouring segments. No wording reproduced.
